# The budget {background-color="#0C234B"}

## Four terms, one basin

Tuesday's model: 20,000 m³/d wellfield, uniform recharge, constant heads on the
east and west edges.

| Term | m³/d |
|---|---|
| recharge in | +17,400 |
| net constant-head in | +2,600 |
| **wells out** | **−20,000** |
| discrepancy | 0.00 % |

::: {.fragment}
And here is the sentence that took a model to write: *of the 20,000 m³/d pumped,
17,400 comes from recharge and 2,600 is captured from flow that would otherwise
have left the basin.*
:::

## You predicted that number

Before running anything, in Tuesday's lab:

```python
n_active_cells = (ibound > 0).sum()            # 2320, not 2400
total_recharge = RECHARGE * n_active_cells * DELR * DELC
deficit = -WELL_Q - total_recharge             # 2600
```

::: {.fragment}
**Recharge landing on a constant-head cell is discarded** — MODFLOW applies `RCH`
only where `ibound > 0`. That is 80 cells and 600 m³/d.
:::

::: {.fragment .due-notice}
Predicting the budget before you run is how you find out that your model is doing
something you did not intend. The 600 m³/d is small; the *habit* is not.
:::

## Your turn: close a budget

A model reports these terms. One is missing — work out what it must be.

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_close
recharge_in = 17400.0
constant_head_in = 131774.6
constant_head_out = 129174.6
wells_out = 20000.0
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_close
total_in = ______
total_out = ______
discrepancy_pct = 100 * (total_in - total_out) / ((total_in + total_out) / 2)
print(f"in {total_in:,.1f}  out {total_out:,.1f}  discrepancy {discrepancy_pct:+.4f} %")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_close"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Every `_in` term goes on one side, every `_out` term on the other. There are two
of each.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_close"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```python
total_in = recharge_in + constant_head_in
total_out = constant_head_out + wells_out
```

149,174.6 both ways, discrepancy zero.

Notice how **large the constant-head terms are** — 131,000 m³/d flowing through
the domain, against 20,000 pumped. The regional throughflow dwarfs the well, and
the budget is the only place you see that. It is also a warning: if your boundary
conditions are wrong, they are wrong about the biggest number in the model.
:::
:::

# Depletion vs capture {background-color="#AB0520"}

## Two ways to produce water

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Depletion**

Water taken out of storage.

A one-off withdrawal from the aquifer's stock. Not renewable.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Capture**

Recharge or throughflow diverted to the well.

Renewable — but it was going somewhere, and now it isn't.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .due-notice}
**Neither is free.** "Safe yield" regulation is an argument about how much capture
is acceptable and whose water it was.
:::

## In this model

::: {.incremental}
- Storage is zero — it is steady state, nothing is changing
- So 100% of the well's yield is **capture**
- 17,400 m³/d of captured recharge
- 2,600 m³/d of throughflow that no longer leaves to the north-west
:::

::: {.fragment}
Downstream of this basin, somebody is 2,600 m³/d short and has no way to measure
why. Week 13 adds storage and the picture gets more interesting.
:::

## Your turn: whose water is it?

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_capture
scenarios = {
    "a": "storage — a one-off withdrawal from the aquifer's stock",
    "b": "capture — recharge that would have flowed to the river",
    "c": "capture — throughflow that would have left the basin",
}
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_capture
# A new well starts pumping. After 50 years the aquifer has re-equilibrated
# and heads are steady again. Where is its water coming from?
answer = ______
print(scenarios[answer])
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_capture"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

At steady state, by definition, storage is not changing. So the water cannot be
coming out of storage.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_capture"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

`"b"` or `"c"` — either is right; the point is that it is **not** `"a"`.

Once heads are steady, storage contributes exactly zero by definition. Every
litre the well produces is being taken from somewhere else in the budget: a
river, a spring, a wetland, a neighbour's throughflow, or evapotranspiration that
no longer happens.

**A well at steady state is not "using up" an aquifer. It is redirecting a flux.**
Which flux, and to whose cost, is what the budget tells you and nothing else
does.
:::
:::

# Comparing with reality {background-color="#0C234B"}

## Head is not depth to water

MODFLOW reports head as an **elevation**. A well measures **depth below land
surface**.

$$\text{depth to water} = \text{land surface} - \text{head}$$

::: {.fragment}
Which means every comparison with a real measurement depends on a land-surface
array MODFLOW knows nothing about.
:::

## Your turn: convert head to depth

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_dtw
land_surface_m = 745.0     # at this well's location
modelled_head_m = 661.6
observed_depth_m = 58.0
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_dtw
modelled_depth = ______
residual = ______
print(f"modelled depth to water {modelled_depth:.1f} m")
print(f"observed                {observed_depth_m:.1f} m")
print(f"residual (model - obs)  {residual:+.1f} m")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_dtw"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Depth counts downward from the land surface, so it is the land surface *minus*
the head. The residual convention is modelled minus observed, as in Week 9.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_dtw"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```python
modelled_depth = land_surface_m - modelled_head_m
residual = modelled_depth - observed_depth_m
```

83.4 m modelled against 58.0 m observed — the model puts the water table **25 m
too deep** at this well.

Note that a 25 m head residual is only 0.3% of the elevations involved, which is
why you must never assess a groundwater model by comparing *heads* as numbers.
Compare **residuals**, and compare them against the head *range* across the
domain — 80 m here, so 25 m is over a quarter of the signal.
:::
:::

## Three reasons, none of them bugs

::: {.incremental}
1. **The boundary heads were invented.** 620 m and 700 m, chosen to give a
   plausible gradient. They set the entire head field.
2. **The monitored wells are not a random sample.** They cluster where people
   pump — the valley floor — which is where water is shallowest.
3. **Uniform `K` and uniform recharge.** The real basin has neither.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Reason 2 is the subtle one, and it is the Week 8 sampling problem again. You are
comparing a whole-domain distribution with a biased sample of it.
:::

## What to do about it

::: {.fragment}
**Calibration**: adjust the things you guessed until the model reproduces what you
measured — at the *locations you measured it*, not across the whole domain.
:::

::: {.fragment}
And then be honest about what that gets you. A calibrated model is **one
consistent explanation** of the observations, not the truth. Several different
parameter sets will fit equally well and disagree about the future.
:::

::: {.fragment .due-notice}
That is what Project 3 is about, and why it asks for a comparison of scenarios
rather than a single prediction.
:::
